16.0.s.en: (1) The rebellion against Moses and Aaron

16.0.0.en: Korah was the son of Izhar, and Izhar was the brother of Amram, the father of Moses and Aaron; therefore Korah was the cousin of Moses and Aaron. He was the ringleader of the rebellion and the sad events that followed. There shared with him in this rebellion, from the tribe of Reuben, Dathan, Abiram and On. However, On is not mentioned afterward in the events of the rebellion and murmuring, and so it is likely that he withdrew, turned back and repented after first taking part in the revolt. The tents of the Kohathites were beside the tents of the Reubenites, and perhaps this helped them to agree on the revolt against Moses and Aaron. Korah demanded the priesthood because he was of the tribe of Levi and a cousin of Moses, while the Reubenites, who were the descendants of the firstborn, demanded the leadership of the people in place of Moses, in addition to making the priesthood general among all the tribes. They were followed by two hundred and fifty men (v. 2) of the princes or leaders in the various tribes. All demanded the priesthood, and perhaps they were demanding the return of the priesthood to every family, so that its head would be the priest, as it was before the age of Moses.

16.1.0.en: Princes of the assembly: that is, among the most famous people at the level of the nation.

16.1.1.en: Famous in the congregation: that is, men of standing, who are summoned to attend the important assemblies of the people. Korah and those with him (v. 1) gathered with two hundred and fifty of the most famous personalities of the people and men of standing, “men of renown.” This verse makes clear that this alliance had only one purpose, which was to resist Moses and Aaron.

16.2.0.en: The motive of this murmuring was jealousy, malice and envy, and therefore Korah and those with him could not hide their feelings, and they confronted Moses and Aaron with the words “.. Ye take too much upon you.” What is meant is: enough of this distinction and this exaltedness and this position that belongs to you two. God is available to the whole people, and He is the One who dwells in the midst of the congregation and sanctifies it, and we have no need of a mediator or a priest. Any one of us can do the work that you two are doing.

16.3.0.en: Moses was grieved and greatly disturbed by what he heard, and he prostrated himself before the Lord, “fell upon his face,” taking refuge, complaining and humbling himself that God might intervene in this grave matter, which was liable to divide the people and scatter their unity.

16.4.0.en: After this submissive and humble prayer and prostration before God, Moses spoke with Korah and his company, saying that the judgment and the choice belong to God alone. He is the One who decides whom He chooses for His service, and the one whom God chooses He brings near as priest to Himself. Moses also asked Korah and all his company to come the next day before the Lord carrying their censers, imitating the priests who carry censers of incense before God. Perhaps they had censers that they used in their family worship before the descent of the law of Moses, when the head of the family was its priest.

16.5.0.en: Moses also asked them to light their censers when they came the next day and put incense in them to offer before God, and God is the One who decides whether He accepts their offering of incense or not. The expression “Ye take too much upon you,” ye sons of Levi, expresses Moses' displeasure at their stand, and he knows that they are deceived by Satan and are asking for what is not theirs and what God did not allow. By sons of Levi he means Korah and those of the tribe of Levi who follow him.

16.5.1.en: Among the important spiritual lessons we draw from the preceding verses:

16.5.2.en: 1- The enemy of good may use the nearest of relatives, “the cousin,” to fight a man, and then the war is dangerous and very embarrassing.

16.5.3.en: 2- We also learn that the war of jealousy, if it is not suppressed in its cradle, takes control of a man and his feelings, and his later actions expose him.

16.5.4.en: 3- The spiritual man, facing a fierce war, finds no solution except to prostrate himself before God, humbling himself that He may deliver him.

16.5.5.en: 4- How sweet it is for a man to empty himself and leave judgment and retribution to God the Almighty.

16.6.s.en: (2) Moses' attempt to calm the rebellion

16.6.0.en: Moses spoke first with Korah and his followers of the tribe of Levi, trying to contain the crisis and give them counsel. He addressed them, saying: Why this rebellion? Did God not choose you apart from the other tribes, distinguish you, and give you the honor of serving His house and its contents apart from the others? This is a very high honor, and yet with all this you were not content, but dared to ask for the service of the priesthood which God assigned to Aaron and his sons alone. What you are doing now is a transgression of the divine order and purpose.

16.7.0.en: Moses here draws the attention of Korah and his followers and warns him that what he is doing is murmuring, objection and revolt against God Himself, and not against Aaron, who has nothing in his hand except that he carries out the divine ordinance that God had already declared.

16.8.0.en: After speaking with Korah and the Levites, Moses, the faithful servant, wished to do the same and counsel Dathan and Abiram of the tribe of Reuben, so he called them to meet him. But they proudly refused to meet him, declaring strongly their hatred and malice and their insistence on demanding the priesthood.

16.9.0.en: Their reply was devoid of all decency and courtesy, and went beyond this to sheer impudence. Their reply to Moses was: Have you forgotten that you are the cause of our coming out of a land of good things, “Egypt,” and have brought us to the barren wilderness of Sinai in order to lord it over us as a ruler instead of Pharaoh? Of course their words were pure slander, for Egypt was a land of humiliation, slavery and forced labor. Their words also show their rebellion and their forgetting of the strong hand of God in the ten plagues and the parting of the sea. This was also blasphemy, because God did not bring them out to make them die but that they might inherit the land of promise, which flows with milk and honey; but because of their many murmurings God punished them by postponing their entry into this land.

16.10.0.en: Dathan and Abiram continue their objection to answering Moses' invitation to speak with him, saying, in the form of an accusation against Moses, that he had not fulfilled what he promised either: where is the land with its fields, its goods and its vineyards...? They put a question to Moses, “wilt thou put out the eyes of these men?!” The meaning is: can you blind this people so that it does not see the truth of the bad state we are in in the wilderness? You, then, are the cause and the one responsible for all this, and therefore we will not come up to talk with you about anything.

16.11.0.en: Moses was very displeased at the words of Dathan and Abiram, and instead of entering with them into a fruitless argument, he lifted his heart to God and prayed, asking that God not regard the offering of these rebels. He addressed God, saying: You know, O my God, that I am innocent of all their false accusations, that I have not wronged any of my people, and that I have not taken from these rebels anything, not even one ass.

16.12.0.en: Since Moses found no benefit in this last attempt at counsel, he asked Korah and all those with him in his revolt to gather the next day, with Aaron also, before the Lord, and that every man take his censer lit and carry incense to offer before God. He specifies that the number of men taking part in this rebellion was two hundred and fifty men.

16.12.1.en: We take from Moses a wonderful example in facing problems. Moses was wronged in all the false accusations directed at him, which no man could bear, but in all his affairs he turned to God in prayer. We too may be wronged, and an unexpected war may face us that shakes our being, but we have nothing but the closet on which to rely and from which to receive our help. God, who hears our prayer in secret, rewards us openly, shows forth the truth and gives us comfort.

16.13.s.en: (3) Standing before God and the divine retribution

16.13.0.en: In pride and incitement, Korah did not gather only the two hundred and fifty, but gathered with them very many of the people, “all the congregation.” The two hundred and fifty stood carrying strange fire and incense in their censers, while the fire of Aaron's censer was holy. When all the congregation gathered, the glory of the Lord appeared to all, most probably in the form of the pillar of cloud.

16.14.0.en: The Lord spoke with Moses and Aaron and commanded them not to stand in the midst of the congregation but to get away from it, because God was determined to destroy them. Despite the disobedience of Korah, we find the heart of Moses, the intercessor for his people, speaking with God again and asking Him to forgive them, asking God not to take the sin of one man and repay all the people for it, because the evil of the people was far less than the evil of the one who incited them.

16.15.0.en: After this intercessory prayer of Moses, we find that the Lord answered him and commanded him to counsel the people to move away from the crowd and the gathering around Korah, Dathan and Abiram, and that the congregation not even approach their dwellings.

16.16.0.en: Wicked men: the unjust or the tyrants.

16.16.1.en: In (v. 12) Moses asked Dathan and Abiram to come up to him and speak with him, and despite their refusal he here goes himself to the place where they lived and takes with him some of the elders of the people as witnesses. At the command of the Lord he addressed all the congregation dwelling beside the tents of Dathan and Abiram, calling on them to leave the whole area and not to mingle with them or touch anything of the belongings of Dathan and Abiram, so that they might escape the divine anger and the retribution that would come swiftly.

16.17.0.en: The people responded to the call of Moses and moved away, and all the household of Dathan and Abiram also came out of their tents, from the greatest to the least, and each stood outside his tent at its door.

16.18.0.en: In the strength of a servant confident in his God, Moses began to speak, saying to all the congregation: If these men, that is, Dathan and Abiram and all who belong to them, live a natural life and also die a natural death, then I am not a prophet or one sent from God to you. But if the Lord makes a new thing and the earth opens and swallows up all these into it, this will be the strong sign of their wickedness and the fitting punishment for what these men did in despising the Lord and exalting themselves against Him.

16.19.0.en: Moses had hardly finished speaking when the earth indeed split as he had said, in a frightening and terrifying scene, and swallowed up Dathan and Abiram and all their households, as well as all the possessions of Korah and his family. However, Korah was not among those who perished in this scene, as we shall see later in (v. 35).

16.20.1.en: When they went down into the depths of the earth alive and it closed again, and as the cries of their voices rose when they went down, the whole congregation of the people was afraid and fled far away, as a kind of psychological reaction to this very terrifying scene, and they said to themselves: Let us flee far away, lest the earth swallow us up also.

16.21.0.en: As for the second scene, which was before the tabernacle of the congregation, where Korah and the two hundred and fifty men were gathered with their censers, who wanted to seize the priesthood for themselves in foolish jealousy, the punishment of the Lord was also severe on them, for a fire came out from the Lord and burned them alive. Of course there was also a great fear among the people, like the earlier fear when the earth opened and swallowed up the living. Korah was burned with these men, as is mentioned in (ch. 26:10), but the sons of Korah feared God and did not walk in the disobedience of their father, so they escaped the divine punishment, as is mentioned in (ch. 26:11). Holy men appeared from the sons of Korah, such as the prophet Samuel (1 Chr 6:28) and Heman the psalmist (Job 6:33), and this confirms that whoever obeys God escapes His wrath and is even blessed by Him with many blessings.

16.21.1.en: Moses combined the loving heart that intercedes for its people with the decisive leader in the face of wrong, especially wrong directed at God and His worship. So is the faithful servant and priest: his heart is wide with love and sympathy for all his people, but in what concerns the rights of God, the faith of the Church and the order of its worship and rite, he neither yields nor neglects, because he is entrusted by God with all these.

16.22.0.en: The Lord gave Moses a new command, which was to tell Eleazar the priest, the son of Aaron, to gather the censers that remained after all had perished in the fire and to scatter the dust and ashes remaining in them. God makes clear that, despite the error of these men, these censers had been hallowed by the fire coming out from God and burning them.

16.23.0.en: Sinners against their own souls: that is, those who sinned and thereby brought punishment on themselves. God commanded Moses to beat out these censers for a covering of the altar of burnt offering, because they had been hallowed by being offered to God. It would be a sign to the children of Israel, a memorial never to be forgotten, of what the rebels, the leaders of the rebellion, had done and how their end came. Eleazar did exactly as Moses commanded him.

16.24.0.en: Stranger: one of the common people, but not of the descendants of Aaron, who was called to the priesthood.

16.24.1.en: God makes clear again here the purpose, that this covering of brass on the altar is to be a warning memorial for the children of Israel, that no stranger come near and dare to offer incense before the Lord, lest his end be like the end of Korah, to whom Moses spoke and who took no heed and did not listen to his words.

16.24.2.en: Remember your great sins into which you fell long ago and which God forgave you, so that you may humble yourself before Him, take care of your repentance every day, guard against these sins, and strive to acquire the virtues opposed to them.

16.25.s.en: (5) The people's murmuring against Moses and Aaron and God's punishment of them

16.25.0.en: Despite the clear gravity of the sin of rebellion before the eyes of all the people, they fell into murmuring against Moses for the death of Korah and those with him, forgetting that this was the justice of God and their necessary recompense.

16.26.0.en: Facing this new revolt, Moses and Aaron found no protection from the evil of the people except taking refuge in God and standing at the door of the tabernacle of the congregation. The glory of the Lord came down again, and the sign of this was that the tabernacle was covered with the cloud.

16.27.0.en: The scene was repeated, with almost the same dialogue as in (vv. 21, 22). God asked Moses and Aaron to get away from the congregation until the murmurers were consumed, but we find Moses again prostrating himself before God with his brother Aaron, as a sign of submission on the one hand and an entreaty for divine pardon and forgiveness on the other.

16.28.0.en: Moses knew that God's judgment on the disobedient of His people this time was a deadly, destructive plague that leaves a man only dead. With the same fatherly heart that has pity on the folly of his people, he quickly asked Aaron to take holy fire from the altar and go out with it to all the people and pass among them between their tents, and offer atonement for the people so that God would remove His wrath and stop the plague. Indeed Aaron did exactly as Moses commanded him, put on incense, and prayed an atoning prayer for the people. The word “ran” shows how hasty Aaron was in carrying out the command to stop the plague.

16.29.0.en: When Aaron went down among the people, he stopped the spread of the plague, so that the sick who were dying were on one side and the living, whom Aaron protected, on the other. Aaron stood with his censer between the dead and the living, in a beautiful picture that makes his priesthood, his prayer and his incense a barrier that prevents the evil of the punishment of sin from reaching the rest of his people. We see that God answered this priestly, intercessory work, so the plague stopped and spread no further, and there appeared before all the people the greatness of the priesthood and its effectiveness in protecting from death, this priesthood confined to Aaron and his sons. So they honored the priesthood and feared God, Moses and Aaron.

16.30.0.en: The price of sin was heavy and the loss great, for the number who died in the plague because of the second murmuring was fourteen thousand and seven hundred, while those who died in the first punishment were Korah, the two hundred and fifty, and the households of Dathan and Abiram.

16.31.0.en: This chapter ends by declaring the end of the sad events and the return of things to their first state after the plague was lifted and Aaron returned to Moses, who had remained standing, awaiting the mercies of God, at the door of the tabernacle.

16.31.1.en: My beloved brother... how evil it is for a man not to accept God's warnings and punishment, but to persist in his disobedience and murmuring, and so bring on himself a punishment worse and graver than the first. So be quick to return and repent, and go to your father the priest in repentance to receive God's mercies and pardon, instead of continuing in evil, lest there come upon you a divine wrath that you cannot bear.

16.31.2.en: Introduction to Aaron's rod and the rods of the tribes: After the events of the preceding rebellion and God's punishment of the murmurers, God wished to give a sign to His people by which to prove the distinction of Aaron and his priesthood from the rest of the tribes.
